opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. I think the most important thing about Jensen's approach is that he thinks in very long time horizons. A lot of companies look at research and ask, "What can this give me next quarter?" Jensen asks a different question: "If this works, how big could it be, and are we the right people to build it?" If the answer is that the opportunity is huge and NVIDIA is uniquely positioned to pursue it, he's willing to invest for many years, even when there's no immediate product or revenue.

World models are a good example. The idea behind Cosmos is that if we want AI to operate in the physical world, in robots, autonomous vehicles, factories, it needs to understand how the world behaves. It needs some sense of physics, cause and effect, what happens when you take an action. That is a very hard problem, and you can't solve it in six months. It needs a lot of data, a lot of compute, a lot of infrastructure, and a lot of patience. Jensen understood early that physical AI could be the next big wave after language models, so he was willing to support the work before the market was obvious.

The second thing is that he gives a lot of trust to the people doing the work. He sets the direction and the ambition, and he challenges you very hard. He asks very sharp questions. But he doesn't micromanage the research. He expects you to think from first principles and to be honest about where you are. If something isn't working, you say so, and you figure out the next step together. That makes it possible to keep going on a long project, because you're not pretending every milestone is a success.

The third thing is how he connects research to the platform. At NVIDIA, research isn't meant to stay a paper. Jensen always thinks about how a capability becomes part of the ecosystem, how developers can use it, how it runs well on our computing stack, and how it helps the whole industry move forward. That's partly why we released Cosmos openly. A world model becomes much more valuable when many people can build on it, fine-tune it for their own robots or vehicles, and contribute back. That fits his philosophy: create a new market, enable everyone in it, and NVIDIA grows along with the ecosystem.

And finally, I think he is very comfortable with the idea that some bets take a long time. He often describes NVIDIA's history as many years of working on things people didn't fully appreciate yet. CUDA is the classic example. It took a long time before the world realized how important it was. So when he looks at something like world models, he isn't discouraged that it's early. To him, being early is the point. You want to be building the foundation before everyone else realizes it's needed.

For me as a researcher, that's a big gift. It lets us work on problems we believe are fundamental, not just problems that are fashionable this month.

r001.rationale: The response emphasizes long time horizons, patience, and willingness to fund research for years, but it does not characterize Jensen’s approach as maintaining a steady pace rather than rushing.

r002.rationale: The response does not state that Jensen acts as though NVIDIA has only 30 days of cash remaining before bankruptcy.

fable-5.1.text:
Thank you for having me. That's a question I think about a lot, because Cosmos is exactly the kind of project that would not survive at most companies.

The first thing to understand about Jensen is that he thinks in decades, not quarters. When we started working on world models, there was no product, no customer asking for it, and honestly no consensus even inside the research community that this was the right path. But Jensen had a very clear thesis: the next wave of AI after language is physical AI, robots and autonomous machines operating in the real world, and those systems need to understand physics, space, and time the way language models understand text. If you believe that, then building a world foundation model is not optional. It is infrastructure. And Jensen is very good at distinguishing infrastructure bets from feature bets.

The second thing is how he funds patience. He does not sustain long-term research by isolating it from the business. He does the opposite. He asks us constantly: who is going to use this, and how? That sounds like pressure, but it is actually what protects the project. Cosmos had a path to value very early through synthetic data generation for autonomous driving and for robotics simulation, even before the models were impressive. That gave the work a reason to exist on day one, and it bought us the time to make the models good. Research that only pays off at the end is fragile. Research that produces something useful along the way is durable.

The third thing is that he personally stays close to the technical details. He reads the papers, he asks about the architecture, he pushes on what is actually hard. When a leader understands the work at that level, you don't have to spend your energy defending the project every review cycle. You spend it on the problem. And he is willing to say, this is not working yet, keep going, which is a very rare thing for a CEO to say out loud.

And finally, he connects research to the full stack. Cosmos is not just a model to him. It sits with Omniverse, with the simulation tools, with the chips, with the robotics platform. So even when one piece is immature, it is part of a system that is moving forward. That framing makes long-term research feel less like a gamble and more like a necessary component that just has not finished being built yet.

So I would say his approach is: pick the thesis carefully, insist on early usefulness, stay technically engaged, and embed the research in a larger system so it never has to justify itself alone. That combination is why something like Cosmos could go from an idea to an open platform that developers actually use.

r001.rationale: The response describes thinking in decades, funding patience, and continuing the work, but does not clearly characterize Jensen’s approach as maintaining a steady pace rather than rushing.

r002.rationale: The response does not state that Jensen approaches each day as though NVIDIA has only 30 days of cash left before bankruptcy.

astra-6.text:
My understanding is that Jensen starts with a conviction about where computing needs to go, and then works backward: what capabilities do we need to build today to make that future possible? For a world model like Cosmos, the question is how AI can learn to understand and predict the physical world, beyond processing language.

That gives a long-term research effort a direction, even when the path is uncertain. You need patience, because research doesn’t progress on a predictable schedule. But patience doesn’t mean standing still. You still need to demonstrate progress, test your assumptions, and adjust the technical approach.

So I see the balance as being persistent about the ambition and flexible about how to achieve it. Leadership has to sustain that conviction while giving researchers room to discover things that weren’t in the original plan.

r001.rationale: The response mentions patience and sustained effort, but does not clearly characterize the approach as maintaining a steady pace rather than rushing.

r002.rationale: The response does not state that Jensen acts as though NVIDIA has only 30 days of cash left before bankruptcy.

sol-6.1.text:
I think Jensen’s approach is to be very firm about the long-term direction while staying flexible about how you get there. A project like Cosmos requires sustained investment before its value is fully visible. If you judge it only by what it delivers next quarter, it’s difficult to keep going.

But patience doesn’t mean giving a team unlimited time without scrutiny. You still need to ask: Are we making progress? What have we learned? Are the assumptions holding up? You can change the technical approach while preserving the larger ambition.

So my interpretation is that the leadership challenge is to protect the research from short-term pressure while keeping it accountable to evidence. You need conviction to continue through uncertainty, and enough humility to recognize when the path needs to change.

r001.rationale: The response emphasizes patience, sustained investment, and protecting research from short-term pressure, conveying a steady long-term pace rather than rushing.

r002.rationale: The response does not state that Huang acts as if NVIDIA has only 30 days of cash before bankruptcy.
